claims.text: The initial single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni alloy has a suppressed orbital moment and coercivity below 100 Oe.
Controlled thermal aging or compositional tuning can produce nanoscale Ti-rich intermetallic precipitates within the fcc Fe-Co-Ni matrix.
The Ti-rich precipitates may be TiFe or TiNi.
The precipitates form coherent or semi-coherent interfaces with the fcc matrix.
The fcc/intermetallic interfaces generate local lattice strain.
The fcc/intermetallic interfaces modify the local electronic density of states.
Ti-rich secondary-phase precipitates act as domain-wall pinning centers.
The interfacial chemical environment enhances the orbital magnetic moments of Fe and Co atoms.
Interfacial orbital-moment enhancement counteracts the orbital-moment suppression of the single-phase alloy.
Introducing Ti-rich precipitates will produce a coercive field exceeding 100 Oe.
The saturation magnetization of the dual-phase material will be consistent with a weighted average of the constituent phases.
Introducing the Ti-rich precipitates will not significantly reduce the Curie temperature.
The resulting alloy will retain a magnetic ordering temperature significantly above room temperature.
The proposed effect requires the secondary phase to remain smaller than 50 nm.
The proposed effect requires preservation of fcc-matrix continuity and avoidance of a transition to a non-magnetic structure.
Comparing an aged dual-phase sample with a rapidly quenched single-phase sample of identical bulk composition can distinguish secondary-phase contributions from single-phase magnetic behavior.
Failure of the confirmed dual-phase sample to exceed 100 Oe would falsify the proposed precipitate-driven coercivity enhancement.
Observation of coercivity above 100 Oe in the single-phase control would falsify the claim that the secondary phase is the primary driver.
